item.title: LLMs, scripts, and semi-automated conversations
item.lead: The source describes LLMs as a next step in an already existing script culture: the machine can produce variants of human-sounding answers faster.

blocks.text: Scripts provide structure: greeting, relationship building, objection handling, upsell, and retention. A language model can then generate multiple variants within such a structure. This allows the human operator to handle more conversations simultaneously, or respond more quickly to unexpected questions.

The source links this to CRM profiles. When a model knows that a user has previously shared a certain event or preference, it can connect to that. From a technical point of view, this is a form of context injection; from the moral framework of the dossier, it is a form of automated personalization of vulnerability.

It is important that automation does not automatically imply deception. A chat assistant can be used transparently for summarization, translation, or customer service. The problematic boundary arises, according to the dossier, when the user reasonably believes to be communicating with a unique person, while an automated or shared backend effectively determines the interaction, and the user has no insight into this.
The technical boundary is therefore simultaneously a transparency boundary. The core question becomes: what degree of automation can be compatible with a justified expectation of human proximity?
